title: Degree and Radian Measure
learningObjective: Convert between degrees and radians. Draw angles in standard position.

faqs.question: What is an angle, and what are the initial side, terminal side, and vertex?
faqs.answer:
An angle is formed by two rays joined at a shared starting point, called the vertex. In trigonometry, we think of an angle as a rotation: the initial side is where the angle starts (before any rotation), and the terminal side is where the angle ends up after rotating.

The angle is the rotation from the initial side to the terminal side, pivoting at the vertex. The arc with an arrowhead shows the turn.

faqs.question: What does it mean for an angle to be in standard position?
faqs.answer:
An angle is in standard position when its vertex sits at the origin and its initial side lies exactly along the positive x-axis. This gives every angle a consistent, predictable starting point, which is essential once you start comparing angles or plotting them on the coordinate plane.

Standard position: vertex at the origin, initial side along the positive x-axis; the arc shows the counterclockwise turn to the terminal side.

faqs.question: Why do some angles have a positive measure and others a negative measure?
faqs.answer:
The sign of an angle tells you which direction it was rotated. An angle measured counterclockwise from the initial side is positive; an angle measured clockwise is negative. For example, +60° and −60° are the same amount of rotation in opposite directions; the sign just records which way you turned. Negative angles are an extension, beyond the TR1 CheckIt exercise, which uses only positive angles strictly between 0° and 360°. Keep in mind that the terminal side alone doesn't show the direction or the number of turns: 300° and −60° end on the same side, and only the turn arc tells them apart.

Counterclockwise (teal, labeled +60°, arrow turning up) is positive; clockwise (orange, labeled −60°, arrow turning down) is negative — same size angle, opposite direction.

faqs.question: What is a radian, and how is it actually defined?
faqs.answer:
One radian is the measure of a central angle that cuts out an arc exactly as long as the circle's radius. Picture taking the radius of a circle, bending it around the edge of the circle like a piece of string, and marking where it ends — the angle formed at the center is exactly 1 radian.

When the arc (orange) is exactly as long as the radius, the angle it creates is defined as 1 radian — about 57.3°.

faqs.question: Why are there 2π radians in a full circle?
faqs.answer: This comes straight from the circumference formula. The circumference of a circle is C = 2πr — in other words, the full distance around the circle is always 2π times the radius. Since one radian is defined as the angle created by an arc equal to one radius (see "What is a radian, and how is it actually defined?"), and the whole circle's arc length is 2π radii, a full circle must measure exactly 2π radians.

faqs.question: How do I convert an angle from degrees to radians?
faqs.answer:
Multiply the degree measure by π/180°. This works because 180° and π radians represent the exact same amount of rotation (half a circle), so π radians/180° is just a conversion factor equal to 1.
Worked Example

Convert \( 210^\circ \) to radians:

\( 210^\circ \times \dfrac{\pi}{180^\circ} = \dfrac{210\pi}{180} = \dfrac{7\pi}{6} \)

faqs.question: How do I convert an angle from radians to degrees?
faqs.answer:
Multiply the radian measure by 180°/π — the same conversion factor as in degrees to radians, just flipped upside down since you're converting in the opposite direction.
Worked Example

Convert \( \dfrac{3\pi}{2} \) to degrees:

\( \dfrac{3\pi}{2} \times \dfrac{180^\circ}{\pi} = \dfrac{540^\circ}{2} = 270^\circ \)

faqs.question: How do I sketch an angle in standard position if I'm given its measure in degrees?
faqs.answer:
Start by drawing the initial side along the positive x-axis. Then estimate what fraction of a full circle (360°) the angle represents, and rotate the terminal side that fraction of the way around — counterclockwise if positive, clockwise if negative. You don't need to be perfectly precise, but CheckIt's TR1 angles are multiples of 30° or 45°, so aim for the right 30° or 45° mark, not just the right quadrant: 300° and 330° are both in Quadrant IV but are different drawings.
Worked Example

Sketch \( 120° \): since \( 120° \) is a bit more than a quarter turn (90°) but less than a half turn (180°), rotate the terminal side counterclockwise into Quadrant II, 30° past the positive y-axis, so closer to the positive y-axis than to the negative x-axis.

faqs.question: How do I sketch an angle in standard position if I'm given its measure in radians?
faqs.answer: Convert the radian measure to degrees first (multiply by 180°/π) if that helps you visualize it, or use benchmark radian angles you're building familiarity with: π/2 is a quarter turn, π is a half turn, 3π/2 is three-quarters of a turn, and 2π is a full circle. Then estimate where your angle falls relative to those benchmarks.

faqs.question: How do I know which direction to draw an angle — clockwise or counterclockwise?
faqs.answer: Check the sign. A positive angle measure always means counterclockwise rotation from the initial side; a negative angle measure always means clockwise rotation. If no sign is written, assume positive (counterclockwise). Negative angles are an extension, beyond the TR1 CheckIt exercise, which uses only positive angles strictly between 0° and 360°.

faqs.question: Why do radian measures often involve π, and what does a value like 7π/6 actually mean?
faqs.answer: Since a full turn is exactly 2π radians, familiar angles have measures that are convenient fractions of π, so we keep π in the expression rather than converting to a decimal. In 7π/6, each slice measures π/6, or 30°. Six slices make a half turn (π), and twelve make a full turn (2π). Seven slices give 210°, which puts the terminal side 30° past the negative x-axis, in Quadrant III. When the angle is written as a fraction of π, the denominator tells you how many equal slices make a half turn; the numerator tells you how many of those slices you rotate through. Reading radians this way makes them much easier to picture. (Radian measures don't have to contain π; 1 or 2 radians are angles too. The angles in the TR1 CheckIt exercise are multiples of π/6 or π/4, such as π/6, 3π/4 and π itself (CheckIt writes 180° as just π).)

faqs.question: How does everything in TR1 set up the rest of the trig unit?
faqs.answer: Standard position and the degree/radian relationship are the language every later trig topic is written in. TR2's coterminal angles only make sense once you understand rotation and standard position. TR3's right-triangle trig and TR5's unit circle both rely on angles being placed and measured consistently. Radians specifically become essential once you reach calculus, where trig functions are almost always used with radians.

faqs.question: Why do radians matter beyond just being another unit for angles?
faqs.answer: Radians aren't just a different way to write the same angle — they connect an angle directly to actual distance along a circle, since the radian definition is built from arc length and radius. Radians make these relationships especially simple: arc length is \( s=r\theta \) when \( \theta \) is in radians, with no extra conversion factor, and angular velocity works the same way. Degrees can describe these quantities too, but only with a conversion factor. Radians also give the standard forms of the calculus formulas for trig functions.

guided.title: Practice Standard Position
guided.prompt: I'm practicing drawing angles in standard position for my TR1 CheckIt. Give me one angle at a time, chosen from the special angles strictly between 0° and 360° that are multiples of 30° or 45° (30°, 45°, 60°, 90°, 120°, 135°, 150°, 180°, 210°, 225°, 240°, 270°, 300°, 315°, 330°). Mix the units: give some in degrees and some in radians, written like 5π/6, or just π for 180°. For each one, I'll sketch it on paper and tell you which way I turned, where the terminal side ends (a quadrant or an axis), and how far it is from the nearest axis, past it or short of it. Don't confirm until I explain why. After I've done three, describe your own sketch of a new angle from the same list with one hidden mistake (wrong direction, wrong quadrant or axis, or wrong distance from the nearest axis), and I'll find it using the angle's measure. After I respond, check my reasoning and give me the fully corrected solution before we finish.

guided.title: Understand the Radian Definition
guided.prompt: I'm learning what a radian is. Here is the definition from my notes: one radian is the central angle that cuts off an arc exactly as long as the circle's radius. Start by asking me to restate that in my own words and to estimate roughly how many degrees one radian is. Then ask me questions that lead me to explain why a half turn measures π radians (the circumference is 2πr). Don't explain it for me unless I'm stuck after two tries. Then write a short explanation of why 180° = π radians with one subtle error in it, and I'll find it and check it against my notes. After I respond, check my reasoning and give me the fully corrected solution before we finish.

guided.title: Practice Degree-Radian Conversion
guided.prompt: I'm learning to convert between degrees and radians for my TR1 CheckIt. Pretend you're a classmate. Convert five angles in CheckIt's style: special angles strictly between 0° and 360° that are multiples of 30° or 45°, some given in degrees (convert to radians, written like 5π/6, or just π for 180°) and some given in radians (convert to degrees). Show your work for each one. Get exactly two wrong in realistic ways, choosing for each a mistake that fits its direction: for degrees to radians, multiply by π/360 instead of π/180, or by 180/π instead of π/180; for radians to degrees, multiply by π/180 instead of 180/π, or leave π in the degree answer. Don't tell me which two are wrong. I'll grade all five, find the two mistakes, and explain each fix. After I respond, check my reasoning and give me the fully corrected solution before we finish.

guided.title: Build Intuition for Radian Benchmarks
guided.prompt: I'm trying to build a mental picture of common radian angles like π/2, π, 3π/2, and 2π. Can you help me visualize each one as a fraction of a full turn around a circle? Then give me a radian value like 7π/6 or 5π/4 and help me figure out roughly where it lands without converting to degrees first. Then tell me where 11π/6 and 2π/3 land, getting one wrong, and ask me which one you got wrong and how I know. After I respond, check my reasoning and give me the fully corrected solution before we finish.

guided.title: Extension: Connect Radians to Arc Length
guided.prompt: This goes beyond the TR1 CheckIt exercise (arc length is part of TR2). I've learned that one radian is the central angle whose arc is as long as the radius, so an angle of θ radians cuts off an arc of length r times θ. Before you explain anything, ask me to predict how far a wheel with a 1-foot radius rolls, without slipping, in a half turn and in one full turn. Then help me check my predictions, and point out where my reasoning was right. Then work out how far a wheel with a 2-foot radius rolls in a quarter turn, but make one deliberate mistake in your work. I'll find it and check it against s = rθ. After I respond, check my reasoning and give me the fully corrected solution before we finish.

paths.label: TR1: Degree and Radian Measure
paths.intro: Builds to the TR1 check: drawing angles in standard position and converting between degrees and radians. Practice scope: the guided path focuses on the positive special angles used in the TR1 CheckIt exercise. The optional extension at the end adds negative angles.

stages.desc: Two quick skills TR1 leans on. Skip any you already have.

stops.title: Simplify fractions over 180
stops.target: Reduce fractions like \(\dfrac{270}{180}\) to lowest terms by dividing by common factors.
stops.solution: 120/180: both divide by 60, giving 2/3. 300/180: both divide by 60, giving 5/3. If you do not see the biggest factor, divide by any common factor first (10, 5, 9 or 15 often work), then keep going.
stops.reflect: What is a quick first step when you do not see the biggest common factor?

stops.title: Standard position and quadrants
stops.target: An angle in standard position starts on the positive \(x\)-axis (initial side) and rotates counterclockwise for positive angles. Know which quadrant each range of angles ends in.
stops.cold: In which quadrant (or on which axis) does each angle end? \(120^\circ\), \(300^\circ\), \(210^\circ\)
stops.coldPlain: In which quadrant (or on which axis) does each angle end: 120 degrees, 300 degrees, 210 degrees?
stops.coldA: \(120^\circ\): Quadrant II. \(300^\circ\): Quadrant IV. \(210^\circ\): Quadrant III.
stops.solution: Quadrant I is strictly between 0 and 90 degrees (0 < θ < 90), II is 90 < θ < 180, III is 180 < θ < 270, and IV is 270 < θ < 360. Angles of 0, 90, 180 and 270 degrees land on an axis, not in a quadrant. So 120 is in II, 300 in IV, and 210 in III.
stops.mistake: Counting quadrants clockwise, or starting from the y-axis.
stops.againA: \(60^\circ\): Quadrant I. \(270^\circ\): on the negative \(y\)-axis (not in a quadrant). \(170^\circ\): Quadrant II.
stops.reflect: Which four angles from 0° up to (but not including) 360° have terminal sides on the coordinate axes?

stages.desc: One stop per skill on the TR1 check: drawing angles and converting both ways.

stops.title: Draw a degree angle
stops.target: Draw an angle in degrees in standard position: start on the positive \(x\)-axis, turn counterclockwise, and use the nearest axis as a landmark: turn the extra amount past it, or stop the right amount short of it.
stops.note: I drew the angle on paper. I'll either upload a photo or describe it: where the initial side is, which direction I rotated, which quadrant or axis the terminal side ends in, and how far it is from the nearest axis (past it or short of it). Check my drawing.
stops.coldA: \(315^\circ = 360^\circ - 45^\circ\): stop \(45^\circ\) short of a full turn (the same as \(45^\circ\) past the negative \(y\)-axis), halfway between the negative \(y\)-axis and the positive \(x\)-axis, in Quadrant IV.[[graph:d315]]
stops.solution: Start on the positive x-axis and rotate counterclockwise. 315 is between 270 (the negative y-axis) and 360 (back to the positive x-axis). 315 = 270 + 45 = 360 - 45, so the terminal side is exactly halfway between the negative y-axis and the positive x-axis, in Quadrant IV. Draw the terminal side as a ray, then a small arc with an arrow turning counterclockwise from the positive x-axis all the way around to it, and label the arc 315 degrees.
stops.mistake: Rotating clockwise (a clockwise turn of 315 degrees ends in Quadrant I), or forgetting the arc that shows the rotation. (CheckIt's answer picture draws both sides as rays with arrowheads and marks the angle with a small arc labelled with its measure. Putting an arrow on the arc to show the direction of the turn is still good practice.)
stops.againA: \(60^\circ\) is two thirds of the way from the positive \(x\)-axis to the positive \(y\)-axis (\(30^\circ\) short of the positive \(y\)-axis), in Quadrant I.[[graph:d60]]
stops.stretchA: \(180^\circ + 30^\circ\): \(30^\circ\) past the negative \(x\)-axis, in Quadrant III.[[graph:d210]]
stops.reflect: How do benchmarks like \(90^\circ\), \(180^\circ\), and \(270^\circ\) help you draw quickly?

stops.title: Degrees to radians
stops.target: Convert degrees to radians by multiplying by \(\dfrac{\pi}{180^\circ}\) and simplifying. (\(180^\circ = \pi\) radians.)
stops.solution: Multiply by pi/180: 135 * pi/180 = 135pi/180. Simplify 135/180 = 3/4 (divide by 45). Answer: 3pi/4.
stops.mistake: Multiplying by 180/pi (the wrong direction): 135 * 180/pi = 24300/pi, about 7735, which is far too big to be part of one turn.
stops.stretchA: \(90^\circ = \dfrac{90\pi}{180} = \dfrac{\pi}{2}\) and \(180^\circ = \dfrac{180\pi}{180} = \pi\). CheckIt writes the second answer as just \(\pi\), not \(\dfrac{\pi}{1}\) or \(1\pi\).
stops.reflect: How do you remember which fraction to multiply by?

stops.title: Radians to degrees
stops.target: Convert radians to degrees by multiplying by \(\dfrac{180^\circ}{\pi}\). For the multiples of \(\pi\) used here, the \(\pi\) factors cancel.
stops.solution: Multiply by 180/pi. The pi cancels: (4/3)(180) = 240 degrees. Shortcut: when the angle is written as a number times pi, as every CheckIt angle is, you can replace pi with 180 degrees, so 4(180)/3 = 240. This does not work for an angle like 2 radians, which has no pi to replace: 2 * 180/pi is about 114.6 degrees.
stops.mistake: Keeping the pi in the answer.

stops.title: Draw a radian angle
stops.target: Draw an angle in radians by thinking in slices of a half turn (\(\pi\)): \(\dfrac{11\pi}{6}\) is 11 slices of \(\dfrac{\pi}{6}\), one slice short of a full turn (\(2\pi\)).
stops.note: I drew the angle on paper. I'll either upload a photo or describe it: where the initial side is, which direction I rotated, which quadrant or axis the terminal side ends in, and how far it is from the nearest axis (past it or short of it). Check my drawing.
stops.coldA: \(\pi\) is a half turn cut into 6 slices, so a full turn \(2\pi\) is 12 slices; go 11 of them. That is \(\dfrac{\pi}{6}\) short of the positive \(x\)-axis, in Quadrant IV.[[graph:r330]]
stops.solution: Each slice is pi/6, or 30 degrees. pi is 6 slices (a half turn) and 2pi is 12 slices (a full turn). 11pi/6 is 11 slices: one slice short of a full turn, just below the positive x-axis, in Quadrant IV. If it helps, convert: 11pi/6 = 330 degrees.
stops.mistake: Cutting the whole circle into 6 slices instead of the half turn, which makes 11pi/6 look like almost two full turns. (As with degree drawings, CheckIt's answer picture marks the angle with a small arc labelled with its measure. Putting an arrow on the arc to show the direction of the turn is still good practice.)
stops.againA: \(\dfrac{7\pi}{6} = \pi + \dfrac{\pi}{6}\): one \(\dfrac{\pi}{6}\) slice past the negative \(x\)-axis, in Quadrant III.[[graph:r210]]\(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\): halfway to the positive \(y\)-axis, Quadrant I.[[graph:r45]]
stops.reflect: How can comparing a radian angle to \(\pi\) and \(2\pi\) tell you where it lands?
stops.stretch: Draw \(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\) and \(\dfrac{3\pi}{2}\). Where does each terminal side end?
stops.stretchA: \(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\) is a quarter turn, ending on the positive \(y\)-axis.[[graph:r90]]\(\dfrac{3\pi}{2}\) is three quarter turns, ending on the negative \(y\)-axis.[[graph:r270]]Neither is in a quadrant: an angle whose terminal side is on an axis is not in any quadrant.

stages.desc: A practice check in the same two-part format as the TR1 CheckIt exercise.

stops.title: Practice check
stops.target: Draw a degree angle and a radian angle in standard position, and convert each to the other unit.
stops.cold:
(a) Draw the angle \(210^\circ\) in standard position. Convert the angle \(210^\circ\) to radians.
(b) Draw the angle \(\dfrac{3\pi}{2}\) in standard position. Convert the angle \(\dfrac{3\pi}{2}\) to degrees.
stops.coldPlain: (a) Draw the angle 210 degrees in standard position. Convert the angle 210 degrees to radians. (b) Draw the angle 3pi/2 in standard position. Convert the angle 3pi/2 to degrees.
stops.note: I drew both angles on paper. I'll upload a photo, or for each one I'll tell you where it starts, which way I turned, where it ends, and how far it is from the nearest axis (past it or short of it). Check both.
stops.coldA: (a) \(180^\circ + 30^\circ\): \(30^\circ\) past the negative \(x\)-axis, in Quadrant III. \(210^\circ = \dfrac{7\pi}{6}\).[[graph:d210]](b) Three quarter turns: the terminal side lies on the negative \(y\)-axis, in no quadrant. \(\dfrac{3\pi}{2} = 270^\circ\).[[graph:r270]]
stops.solution: (a) 210 = 180 + 30: 30 degrees past the negative x-axis, in Quadrant III. 210 * pi/180 = 210pi/180 = 7pi/6 (divide by 30). (b) Each quarter turn is pi/2, so 3pi/2 is three quarter turns: the terminal side lies on the negative y-axis, not in any quadrant. 3pi/2 * 180/pi = 540/2 = 270 degrees.
stops.mistake: Drawing clockwise, or converting in the wrong direction.
stops.again:
(a) Draw \(135^\circ\) and convert it to radians.
(b) Draw \(\dfrac{11\pi}{6}\) and convert it to degrees.
stops.againA: (a) \(90^\circ + 45^\circ\): halfway between the positive \(y\)-axis and the negative \(x\)-axis, in Quadrant II. \(135^\circ = \dfrac{3\pi}{4}\).[[graph:d135]](b) \(2\pi - \dfrac{\pi}{6}\), Quadrant IV. \(\dfrac{11\pi}{6} = 330^\circ\).[[graph:r330]]
stops.reflect: Which is easier for you to picture, degrees or radians? What will help with the other?
stops.stretch: Extension (beyond the TR1 CheckIt exercise): (a) Draw \(-150^\circ\) and convert it to radians. (b) Draw \(-\dfrac{3\pi}{4}\) and convert it to degrees.
stops.stretchA: (a) Rotate \(150^\circ\) clockwise: \(60^\circ\) past the negative \(y\)-axis (\(30^\circ\) short of the negative \(x\)-axis), in Quadrant III. \(-150^\circ = -\dfrac{5\pi}{6}\).[[graph:dn150]](b) Rotate \(\dfrac{3\pi}{4}\) (\(135^\circ\)) clockwise: \(45^\circ\) past the negative \(y\)-axis, in Quadrant III. \(-\dfrac{3\pi}{4} = -135^\circ\).[[graph:rn135]]Notice that \(-150^\circ\) ends on the same side as the \(210^\circ\) you drew in part (a) of the practice check. Only the direction of the turn arc tells them apart.
